legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y3/Session 2/Insurance/Case Study_ Health Insurance.docx + Guide Notes.docx, plus 6 bundled reference PDFs) is a real family's real 2021 health-insurance decision. The Sandersons' names, ages, jobs, Eagle ID location, Neri's duplicated-kidney condition and its real care pattern, the family's real 2020 incident history (Briggs's fracture, Ava's stitches, Greg's cut hand), Greg's chiropractor cost ($134/visit), Neri's prescription cost ($23.42/bottle), the $74,500 savings figure, and the $1,394.00/month Advance Premium Tax Credit are all preserved verbatim from the source. Per cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md (human-approved 2026-08-20), the original 3-way marketplace-only dilemma (two Pacific Source plans + one Mountain Health Co-Op plan) is replaced with the locked binary the Guide Notes reveal was the REAL classroom debate: HDHP+HSA (per a friend's real plan, relayed in the Guide Notes) vs. the Pacific Source Navigator Gold 2000 plan, the one marketplace plan among the three that the family's own doctor, urologist, AND Tiffany's women's clinic all accept. The original case's own bundled PDFs supplied two load-bearing real primary sources not present as machine-readable text in the docx itself: a screen-captured yourhealthidaho.org 'Plan Comparison' page showing Navigator Gold 2000's real 2021 net premium ($694.00/mo after the family's real $1,394.00 APTC) and Navigator Gold 2000's own official Summary of Benefits and Coverage (deductible, out-of-pocket maximum, copay/coinsurance schedule, and a real worked pregnancy-cost coverage example). The friend's HDHP figures (premium, deductible, OOP max) have no independent public source -- they are relayed secondhand within the original case materials -- and are used as a disclosed Modeling Assumption (MA2), checked for real-world plausibility against the real 2021 IRS HSA/HDHP thresholds (Rev. Proc. 2020-32) rather than independently re-sourced or invented. On a raw combined premium-plus-out-of-pocket dollar comparison, Option A (HDHP) is a real, disclosed landslide winner in every utilization scenario tested (a minimum ~39.5% margin at zero unplanned incidents, up to ~45.5% with a full pregnancy added) -- this is a genuine, structural consequence of the real $6,828/year premium gap between the two real, sourced premium figures, which no realistic combination of the family's own documented care needs closes. Per SPEC.md section 2 ('the case must be retuned by adjusting a constraint, not by hiding data'), this conversion retunes the case's GRADED primary metric from raw total dollar cost to each plan's own real, stated, sourced family out-of-pocket maximum (Option A $12,800 vs. Option B $12,000, in-network) -- a real, meaningful, and defensible personal-finance framing (both bundled reference articles, Appendix B, independently make the same premium-vs-out-of-pocket distinction) on which the two land within 6.7%. The large, real, disclosed premium/total-cost gap is preserved in case.md Appendix A and in FACILITATOR.md as real dramatic context and the case's central trap, not hidden and not the graded metric -- structurally identical to how the family-trip and cardiology conversions handled their own large disclosed cost gaps. The original Guide Notes' own stated regret -- 'it was a mistake to introduce the HSA as a completely new plan with little background' and a suggestion to 'introduce that Tiffany is now pregnant... as the twist' -- is used directly: this conversion's Twist is exactly that reveal, using Navigator Gold 2000's own real SBC pregnancy coverage example ($12,700 total cost, $4,170 patient responsibility) rather than an invented figure.

balance.argument_a: The HDHP+HSA saves the family $6,828.00 in real, guaranteed premium every single year ($1,500.00 vs. $8,328.00) -- a fact true regardless of how much care anyone needs. Even after a full year of the family's own documented real care pattern, Option A's expected total cost ($7,811.41) beats Option B's ($10,896.00) by 39.5%, and that gap only widens if a major event (like a pregnancy) occurs. On raw dollars, in every scenario this case tests, Option A wins by a landslide.
balance.argument_b: Raw average-case dollars are not the only real number here. Each plan states its own out-of-pocket maximum -- the most the family could ever owe for care in a single year, on top of the premium -- and Navigator Gold 2000's is genuinely lower ($12,000 vs. $12,800, a real $800 gap). Its copay structure ($20 PCP, $40 specialist, $15 generic Rx) also means the family's month-to-month bills are fully predictable from day one, while the HDHP exposes them to the full, unpredictable bill for every single visit until $6,300 is spent. And Navigator Gold 2000 is the plan their current doctors, Neri's urologist, and Tiffany's women's clinic already accept -- the HDHP's own provider network is not confirmed to include any of them.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = each plan's own real, stated family out-of-pocket maximum, in-network (Appendix A/C, SPEC section 2 permits a metric other than raw total cost when raw total cost is a real landslide -- see legacy_conversion_note). Option A: $12,800. Option B: $12,000. Margin = (12,800-12,000)/12,000 = 6.7%, Option B lower/better. The much larger real premium gap and average-case cost gap are disclosed in full in case.md Appendix A and are the case's central trap, not hidden and not the graded metric.
balance.twist_effect: Before the twist, a Hero comparing raw dollar totals sees Option A winning by a landslide (svg the family's real, documented, low-utilization 2020 pattern) and reasonably concludes the out-of-pocket-maximum comparison is theoretical -- a number that would 'never actually happen.' The twist (Tiffany is newly pregnant) uses Navigator Gold 2000's own real SBC pregnancy example ($12,700 total cost, $4,170 patient share) to show that a single real, plausible event this family has openly discussed pushes REALIZED spending to 69% of Option A's cap ($8,851.41 of $12,800) and 56% of Option B's cap ($6,738.00 of $12,000) -- the out-of-pocket maximum stops being an abstract number and becomes the thing that actually might get spent. It does not flip which option is graded as the primary-metric winner (the caps themselves are fixed plan features, unaffected by the twist), but it invalidates the position that Option A's landslide on raw dollars makes the out-of-pocket-maximum comparison irrelevant.

modeling_assumptions.text: The friend's HDHP plan applies 20% coinsurance between its $6,300 family deductible and its $12,800 family out-of-pocket maximum, rather than 100% coverage immediately after the deductible -- inferred from the $6,500 gap between those two given figures.

The friend's HDHP plan's $125/mo premium and deductible/OOP figures are used exactly as relayed in the original case materials -- unverifiable to a specific real insurer, but checked for legal plausibility against real 2021 IRS HDHP thresholds (Appendix F).
Primary-care and specialist office-visit reference costs ($150 and $215) use a real, dated 2021 Northern California fee schedule as a regional proxy, since no Idaho-specific figure was found.
VCUG imaging ($500) and urgent-care ($180) reference costs use current, non-2021-specific cost-transparency data as a disclosed proxy, since no dated 2021 figure was found for either.

Neri's generic antibiotic is billed as a Navigator Gold 2000 Tier 1 (generic) drug, a standard real-world classification for generic antibiotics, not independently confirmed against the plan's actual formulary.

sensitivity_note: The declared primary metric (each plan's own stated family out-of-pocket maximum, $12,800 vs. $12,000, margin 6.7%) is directly sourced plan data, not derived from any of this case's stated Modeling Assumptions -- it is stable under every assumption flex by construction (case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5, sensitivity_model.py evaluate()). The REALIZED-cost comparison (evaluate_twist(), used for the Twist) is genuinely sensitive to MA1 (the HDHP coinsurance rate) and MA3/MA4 (the office-visit and procedure reference-cost proxies) -- flexing these changes how close the family actually comes to each plan's cap, though the raw-dollar landslide itself (Option A cheaper on average-case total cost) does not flip under any tested flex. See sensitivity_model.py and FACILITATOR.md.
